inputs: Provider-authorized 835 ERA and 837 claim data, initial-payment or denial receipt dates, payer explanations, QPA disclosures, service codes, facility status, network status, and patient cost-sharing allocations under appropriate privacy and security agreements.

Plan funding and ERISA information, applicable state payment-dispute rules, emergency or nonemergency NSA eligibility facts, notice-and-consent records where relevant, and existing negotiation, IDR, or settlement histories.

Authorized-representative and counsel arrangements, current CMS procedures and certified-entity fee schedules, permissible batching criteria, negotiation/filing calendar, and a collection-based contingency agreement defining QPA and initial-payment treatment.
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest commercial out-of-network 835 ERA remittances for emergency, anesthesia, radiology, and eligible specialty surgical services, then screen federal No Surprises Act eligibility under 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-111 and related provider provisions against specified state-law or All-Payer Model rules; ERISA status is relevant but does not alone resolve jurisdiction. An authorized representative, with counsel where legal representation requires it, starts open negotiation within the applicable 30-business-day initiation window, completes the 30-business-day negotiation period, and initiates federal IDR within four business days afterward, batching only disputes that satisfy then-current federal criteria through a certified IDR entity. Charge 20%–30% only on incremental payer cash collected above the contractual QPA floor after nonreimbursed federal administrative and certified-entity fees, also excluding the initial payer payment from new recovery because QPA is a statutory benchmark rather than necessarily the initial payment; track evidence preparation and professional costs separately from submitted offers and awards.
metrics: Collectible dispute base: federally eligible disputed dollars with timely negotiation and IDR rights, separated from billed charges, requested offers, and unpaid awards.

Realized economics: incremental cash above both the initial-payment baseline and contractual QPA floor, net unreimbursed process fees, 20%–30% contingency receipts, and contribution after evidence and representative costs.
Process performance: timely initiation rate, eligible-batch acceptance rate, cost per resolved claim, days from determination to payment, and unpaid-award aging.
operator_plays.name: Federal No Surprises Act Open-Negotiation and Certified-IDR Recovery Desk

platform_risks.detection_metric: Eligibility rejection rate, batch-separation rate, missed-deadline count, and nonreimbursed process cost as a percentage of incremental collections.
platform_risks.failure_mode: Jurisdiction, batching, or timing defects make an apparently profitable federal IDR submission ineligible.
platform_risks.fallback: Separate disputes only where still timely and permitted, use the applicable state process when available, continue permissible payer negotiation, and cease fee-generating submissions with negative expected net recovery.
platform_risks.impact: Disputes are dismissed or delayed, administrative and preparation expenses are stranded, and an award forecast never becomes incremental provider cash.
platform_risks.trigger: State-law review displaces federal IDR, services fail NSA eligibility, a batch violates current criteria, or negotiation and initiation timestamps miss applicable business-day deadlines.

workflow: 1. Reconcile each ERA to its underlying claim and initial-payment or denial receipt date; exclude ineligible services, route disputes governed by applicable state processes appropriately, and verify federal jurisdiction without assuming every ERISA or specialty-surgery claim qualifies.

2. Send the required open-negotiation notice within 30 business days after receipt of initial payment or denial, run the 30-business-day negotiation period, and assemble permissible evidence without using billed charges or prohibited public-payer comparisons.

3. Initiate federal IDR within four business days after negotiation ends, subject to applicable exceptions or extensions; form only currently permissible batches, select a certified entity, and meet offer, fee, and evidence deadlines rather than treating the initiation window as blanket batching authority.

4. Track settlements, determinations, payer payment deadlines, and actual deposits; calculate the fee base as max(0, cumulative comparable payer cash minus max(initial payer payment, contract-defined comparable QPA floor) minus nonreimbursed administrative and certified-entity fees), excluding patient collections and invoicing only after cash arrives.

sections.heading: 1. Define the recovery desk before acquiring a single claim
paragraphs: This business sells disciplined recovery work to physician groups and other eligible providers, not arbitration outcomes to patients. The provider already delivered care and received an initial commercial-plan payment or denial. An authorized recovery desk identifies disputes potentially covered by the No Surprises Act, establishes the correct payment-resolution route, conducts open negotiation, and supports federal independent dispute resolution when negotiation fails. Federal IDR generally uses final-offer selection: the certified entity chooses one party's offer rather than inventing a midpoint. The desk earns an agreed percentage of additional payer cash actually collected after contractual deductions. Baseline provider collections, patient cost sharing, submitted charges, and unpaid awards are outside operator revenue. The useful production unit is therefore an eligible, timely, evidence-supported dispute with positive expected net recovery, not an uploaded claim. Start with one provider group and one service family whose encounter records, remittance files, and payer correspondence can be reconciled. Require written representative authority and a HIPAA business associate agreement before receiving protected health information. Use counsel where representation, contract interpretation, or state practice rules require legal work. A nonlawyer workflow vendor should not silently expand its engagement into unrestricted legal representation.

Jurisdiction is the first economic filter. Emergency services, qualifying nonemergency services from nonparticipating providers at participating facilities, and eligible air-ambulance services have different coverage hooks and factual requirements. Ground ambulance is not simply another federal IDR specialty. Medicare and Medicaid payment disputes do not become federal commercial IDR inventory because an ERA shows an adjustment. Determine the service date, facility participation, provider participation, plan identity, funding arrangement, service category, and whether a specified state law or All-Payer Model Agreement determines the payment amount. ERISA status is relevant but does not independently settle that analysis; state opt-in arrangements and the particular parties also matter. CARC and RARC codes are routing clues, not jurisdiction decisions. An 835 parser can flag a possible underpayment, but the supporting 837, explanation of benefits, plan documents, and clinical record establish what happened. Preserve the original payer payment and separately record the qualifying payment amount, or QPA. The QPA is a statutory benchmark, not necessarily the initial payment and not an automatic entitlement to a particular award. Reject attractive-looking balances when eligibility cannot be established before the applicable deadline. That rejection saves filing expense and protects scarce reviewer capacity.

The chapter maps twelve operating plays: Federal Open-Negotiation and Certified-IDR Recovery; Comparison-Intent Acquisition; Emergency Physician Recovery; Anesthesia Event Reconciliation; Radiology Component Recovery; Neonatal Acuity Evidence; Hospitalist Encounter Recovery; Assistant-Surgeon Documentation; Air-Ambulance Eligibility; State-Route Triage; Cooling-Period Cohort Control; and Post-Award Cash Reconciliation. The first two correspond to the supplied TRACK_1 and TRACK_2 identifiers; the remaining ten are chapter-local execution plays, not additional scorecard candidates. They share a collection ledger but require different eligibility evidence and failure responses. Build five service archetypes rather than presenting every specialty as interchangeable: an integrated recovery desk, a clinical evidence boutique, a jurisdiction-and-deadline service, a post-award collection desk, and a comparison-led acquisition channel. Only the integrated desk necessarily owns the entire contingency engagement. Other archetypes may support it under written subcontracts without multiplying the provider's fee burden. A defensible moat is a repeatable match between a narrow claim inventory and reliable execution, not a claim that automation eliminates professional judgment. Store acceptance criteria, service limitations, and subcontractor responsibilities in the engagement record. Refuse assignments that require unauthorized access, unsupported factual assertions, or patient collection practices inconsistent with applicable protections.

callout.title: Four habits that protect the recovery inventory
callout.body: Veteran desks preserve facts that become expensive to reconstruct after a filing deadline or payment dispute.
items: Capture the initial payment, separately disclosed QPA, receipt timestamp, and source document as distinct fields; never overwrite one with another.
Ask for original 835 files plus adjustment history, because a later reversal can make a screenshot of the first payment economically misleading.
Group work by provider, payer or administrator, service category, and applicable rule version before testing whether any federal batch is permitted.
Keep a separate post-award queue with the determination date, payment deadline, remittance match, and bank confirmation; winning is not collecting.

sections.heading: 2. Recognize earned fees, not provider balances or paper awards
paragraphs: Use a recovery waterfall that an accountant and a physician owner can independently reproduce. Let C equal cumulative payer cash received for the covered dispute and P0 equal the initial payer payment already received. Incremental cash starts at C minus P0, never at submitted charges minus the QPA. If the engagement expressly establishes a higher contractual QPA floor, use the greater of that floor and P0; otherwise do not manufacture an additional threshold. Deduct nonrefundable administrative fees, certified-entity fees that remain unrecovered, and agreed direct casework disbursements before applying the contingency percentage. For example, total payer cash of $5,000 less a $1,000 initial payment, $200 in unrecovered process fees, and $600 in direct external casework leaves $3,200. At 25%, operator fee revenue is $800 and the provider retains $2,400 of that distributable increment. A separately disclosed $1,200 QPA does not change this example unless the contract makes it the floor; that alternative produces a $750 fee. These process-cost amounts illustrate arithmetic, not a current federal fee schedule. Refunds and later payer recoupments require corresponding waterfall adjustments under the engagement's reconciliation terms.

The canonical revenue basis is the operator's earned contingency share, not provider gross collections. Under an ASC 606 analysis, identify the actual customer, promised recovery service, performance obligations, variable consideration, and principal-versus-agent treatment. Receipt of provider money in a clearing account does not make the whole receipt operator revenue. Design the engagement so the contingent service fee becomes earned on qualifying incremental collection, subject to contractual reconciliation; have the accountant document the resulting recognition policy rather than assuming all cash-basis tax rules determine book revenue. Do not record an unpaid determination as earned contingency revenue merely because the offer prevailed. In the canonical scenarios, retained_share is already embodied in earned contingency revenue; applying the contingency percentage again would understate the business. Keep provider-funded external disbursements separate from operator payroll, evidence supervision, software, insurance, and acquisition expense. Direct external costs deducted before the split must not also appear as unreimbursed operator expense. Internal casework costs that the operator actually bears remain expenses when calculating owner profit. This separation prevents both overstated revenue and double-counted costs. Maintain a claim-level audit trail from payer deposit through deductions, fee invoice, remittance to the provider, and any subsequent correction.

Reconcile every annual plan to Formula v2.0 rather than substituting a dramatic award multiple. At an illustrative 25% blended contingency, Conservative requires $440,000 of distributable incremental collections to produce $110,000 of earned revenue; $77,000 of operator expense leaves $33,000 profit. Base requires $2,020,000 to produce $505,000 revenue; $287,850 expense leaves $217,150 profit. Scaled requires $3,600,000 to produce $900,000 revenue; $396,000 expense leaves $504,000 profit. Those collection bases are after the waterfall deductions, and they are not medical practice revenue forecasts. A $2,000 average distributable recovery would require 220, 1,010, and 1,800 collected units respectively; a unit is a financial modeling convention, not permission to batch claims. Teams remain one full-time operator plus two contractors for Conservative and Base, then two full-time staff plus three contractors for Scaled. Startup capital is $10,000–$45,000, with a planning range of $1,800–$10,500 monthly operating overhead and one to four months to a first engagement. That overhead range does not replace the full annual expense budgets, which include variable delivery costs. Reserve working capital for process fees and collection delays before expanding intake.

sections.heading: 3. Choose sub-verticals by evidence quality and recoverable economics
paragraphs: The central TRACK_1 play is nsa_federal_idr_batch_arbitration_contingency. Its economic engine combines structured remittance intake, jurisdiction screening, timely negotiation, admissible evidence, and payment reconciliation. Consider ten separately eligible disputes expected to generate $2,000 each after process costs and direct casework: at a 25% contingency, full collection produces $5,000 of fees. If only seven reach that collected result, fees fall to $3,500 before operator overhead. The original ten disputes are not automatically a permitted batch, and public prevailing-offer statistics cannot supply their collection probability. The certified entity considers the QPA and permissible additional information under the governing rules; it is not required to mechanically select the QPA. Relevant evidence may include documented patient acuity, service complexity, provider training, facility characteristics, market share, and contracting efforts when applicable. Do not submit billed charges, usual-and-customary charge measures, or public payer reimbursement rates as prohibited valuation substitutes. FAIR Health products require field-level scrutiny: a familiar benchmark brand does not make every metric permissible evidence. When expected net recovery turns negative, stop fee-generating submissions, preserve permissible negotiation, and separate disputes only if the applicable rules and remaining deadlines actually allow that fallback.

TRACK_2, competitor_intent_comparison_hijacking, is an acquisition method, not a medical reimbursement method. Build accurate text-only pages answering searches for a competitor's pricing, cancellation process, or comparison with the desk. Use timestamped public pricing citations, independently written migration instructions, and a calculator whose fee basis matches the engagement. Avoid logos, copied trade dress, implied affiliation, and invented competitor terms. Nominative use is fact-specific; truthful comparison and careful trademark review matter more than labeling a page fair use. Treat the supplied 10–18% conversion range as a test hypothesis with a defined denominator. At 1,000 qualified visits, 10% would yield 100 inquiries, not 100 signed provider clients. If 10% of those inquiries sign and acquisition spend is $6,000, cost per signed client is $600; at 18% inquiry conversion with the same closing rate, eighteen clients would cost about $333 each. These are illustrative funnel calculations, not observed results. Validate lead quality against eligible claim inventory before increasing spend. When a pricing source disappears, remove the numerical comparison or obtain a fresh public source. Keep patient information out of landing-page analytics and use a separate protected onboarding channel after engagement.

The sixteen-row matrix below distinguishes service niches from workflow plays. Its dollar examples use hypothetical distributable incremental collections after the defined recovery deductions, so the stated 25% fee never applies to gross charges or baseline payments. Named platforms indicate possible authorized source systems, not vendor endorsements, promised integrations, or evidence that every listed vendor offers arbitration representation. Emergency Physician Recovery favors records with clear emergency-service facts. Anesthesia Event Reconciliation requires accurate units and encounter linkage, while Radiology Component Recovery separates professional from technical billing. Neonatal Acuity Evidence, Hospitalist Encounter Recovery, and Assistant-Surgeon Documentation depend on clinical facts that generic templates frequently miss. Air-Ambulance Eligibility needs its own statutory analysis rather than copying ground-transport procedures. State-Route Triage can save an otherwise wasted filing but cannot revive an expired state deadline. Cooling-Period Cohort Control protects recurring inventory from premature submissions, and Post-Award Cash Reconciliation closes the gap between determinations and deposits. An illustrative forty-file triage cohort avoiding $150 of unrecovered expense per rejected file preserves $6,000; the amount is a screening model, not an official fee. Prioritize reliable records and payer responsiveness over the specialty displaying the largest billed charge.

sections.heading: 4. Build the deadline, evidence, and collection machine before scaling
paragraphs: Implement a state machine with separate dates for payment or denial receipt, open-negotiation initiation, negotiation completion, IDR initiation, entity selection, offer submission, determination, and payment follow-up. Generally, a party initiates open negotiation within thirty business days after receiving the initial payment or denial, the negotiation period lasts thirty business days, and federal IDR initiation follows within four business days after that period ends. The four-day window is not a generic deadline for entity selection or a blanket batching permission. Use the applicable business-day definition and preserve evidence of receipt and delivery; a practice-management posting date can differ from the operative receipt date. Version the calendar rules against current agency instructions, applicable court orders, and available extensions rather than hard-coding assumptions from an old presentation. Require a human reviewer to verify the destination, parties, jurisdiction, notice contents, and deadline before submission. Python's datetime and zoneinfo can support timestamp handling, while an explicit holiday calendar controls business-day calculations. A daily exception report should surface missing receipt evidence, unresolved payer identity, and approaching expirations. Automation that confidently counts from the wrong event destroys value faster than a slower but documented manual calendar.

Batching and the cooling period deserve independent controls. Apply the then-current federal criteria to the actual parties, services, codes, and service dates; shared specialty or similar reimbursement alone does not authorize a batch. Following a determination, the initiating party generally faces a ninety-calendar-day restriction on initiating another dispute involving the same other party and the same or similar items or services. The rules provide a subsequent submission mechanism for affected disputes, including a thirty-business-day period after the restriction ends; confirm applicability and prerequisites for each cohort instead of treating it as a universal deadline extension. Track each certified entity's published fee and the governing administrative fee schedule at commitment time. Administrative fees are generally nonrefundable. Entity-fee refunds and allocations depend on prevailing status and applicable settlement or dismissal rules; never budget an ineligible or losing dispute as though a refund were assured. After a determination, track the applicable payment deadline, generally thirty calendar days, and reconcile actual deposits. Escalate delayed payment through documented payer follow-up, appropriate agency complaint channels, and counsel where enforcement requires legal action. An aging award is a collection problem, not fresh earned fee revenue.

The small-team advantage depends on separating machine work from accountable judgment. Parse 835 segments, normalize CARC and RARC codes, identify candidate plan types, assemble timelines, and draft evidence indexes automatically. Treat the ERISA classifier as a triage aid whose outputs retain source evidence and confidence, not as a final jurisdiction engine. Have a trained reviewer decide legal routing and a qualified clinical reviewer validate medical assertions. Under 45 CFR § 164.504(e), the business associate agreement must address permitted uses, safeguards, subcontractors, and required reporting. Implement role-based access, minimum-necessary data handling, audit logs, secure transmission, retention controls, and incident procedures appropriate to the records and engagement. Evaluate every external evidence or language processing service before transmitting protected information; a convenient upload button does not establish permitted use. Report a weekly funnel of screened, eligible, negotiated, filed, decided, collected, reversed, and invoiced units, with dollars at each stage. Compare collected fee contribution against actual staff time and acquisition cost by provider cohort. Expand only when another trained reviewer can reproduce the decisions from the retained file. The moat is transferable operating discipline, not dependence on one person's memory.

sop_steps.action: Receive authorized 835 and 837 records, payer notices, plan evidence, and clinical documentation.

Within the volume's 12 mapped plays, this chapter operationalizes medical contingency recovery and factual citation-led acquisition. The provider hires the operator; the responsible plan or issuer funds covered claim obligations; an administrator may merely transmit payment. Separate those roles before accepting inventory. Conservative, Base, and Scaled annual owner profits are $33,000, $217,150, and $504,000 on earned contingency revenue of $110,000, $505,000, and $900,000. sections.heading: 1. Identify the provider buyer, the funded obligor, and the person who can release cash
paragraphs: The provider writes the operator's check, while the responsible health plan or issuer pays the underlying covered claim. A surgical center's CFO buys recoveries because aged underpayments consume working capital, internal collectors lack specialized dispute capacity, and missed filing windows destroy otherwise actionable inventory. The revenue-cycle director evaluates evidence quality and workload; treasury controls bank instructions; procurement signs vendor terms; privacy personnel validate access to protected health information. For a self-funded employer plan, a recognizable insurer logo may identify only the third-party administrator, not the entity bearing benefit expense. For insured coverage, the issuer generally bears that expense, subject to the actual policy and applicable jurisdiction. Obtain the plan identifier, funding classification, administrator delegation, claim number, and payment contact before estimating recovery. An arbitrator decides an eligible dispute but does not insure collection or supply settlement capital. A successful sales meeting therefore ends with two authority maps: who can bind the provider to a contingency agreement, and who can resolve and fund the payer obligation. Ask for an actual remittance example and a recent payment trace rather than accepting a payer directory entry as proof of operational authority.

The acute payer pain is an enforceable payment obligation combined with dispute expense, documented administrative burden, and potential regulatory scrutiny, not embarrassment from an aggressive demand letter. For eligible federal IDR disputes, the selected offer establishes the out-of-network rate; the payment calculation must still reconcile prior payments and lawful patient cost sharing. Under 45 CFR § 149.510, payment following the determination is generally due within 30 calendar days. Do not convert that deadline into a forecast that every award becomes cash on day thirty. Provider executives care about net dollars and forecast reliability, so show award date, payment deadline, trace status, disputes, and collected balance separately. Payer negotiators care about authority limits, repeatable evidence, and avoiding avoidable certified-entity expense; give them an offer supported by claim-specific facts and an executable settlement document. Escalation should identify the missed obligation and competent oversight channel, rather than threaten collection from the patient. Protected patients are not the reserve account for an unpaid payer award. Maintain existing patient protections and correct any patient ledger allocation affected by a settlement. The operator's commercial leverage comes from a complete, timely, collectible file, not from shifting prohibited balance bills onto households.

The first specified play, hospital_lien_medical_receivables_arbitrage, operates here as Out-of-Network Medical Claim & ERISA Appeal Contingency Recovery, with a 20–35% contractual share. Its identifier does not create a hospital lien or authorize attaching patient assets. Recruit surgical centers, specialty clinics, and ambulance businesses only after separating eligible service categories. Ground ambulance claims generally fall outside the federal No Surprises Act balance-billing and IDR framework; air ambulance disputes have distinct provisions, including 45 CFR § 149.520. Nonparticipating facility and clinician claims also require service-setting and coverage analysis. For an illustrative $10,000 initial payment followed by $8,000 additional collected cash, deduct $800 of unrecovered dispute charges and agreed external casework costs, leaving a $7,200 contingency base. At 25%, earned operator revenue is $1,800; the provider retains $5,400 of net incremental recovery, plus its original payment. The $18,000 total payer cash is neither operator revenue nor profit. If the IDR window has expired, evaluate available ERISA benefit appeals under the governing plan and 29 CFR § 2560.503-1. That fallback requires an actual appealable benefit issue, standing, and a live deadline; an administrative appeal cannot simply resurrect a forfeited federal rate-dispute window.

sections.heading: 2. Build jurisdiction, deadline, and fee economics into the same claim ledger
paragraphs: Build the intake record from the 837 claim, 835 electronic remittance, explanation of benefits, clinical documentation, service location, network status, and relevant plan information. CARC and RARC combinations identify investigative leads; they do not establish federal jurisdiction or prove that every denial is an arbitrable payment-rate dispute. Determine whether a specified state law or applicable All-Payer Model controls the payment amount before selecting federal IDR. ERISA status alone does not resolve every jurisdiction question, particularly where state opt-in arrangements or service-specific exceptions matter. Record the initial payment or denial receipt date, the open-negotiation notice delivery evidence, and the parties receiving it. Distinguish the period for initiating open negotiation from the negotiation period itself: federal procedures generally allow initiation within 30 business days after initial payment or denial, followed by a 30-business-day open-negotiation period. The subsequent IDR initiation window is generally four business days. That four-day window is not a universal deadline for selecting the certified entity or assembling every batch. Use a jurisdiction-specific calendar with federal holidays, documented triggering events, and current applicable extensions. A missing date must create a research task, not a fabricated deadline that silently consumes a provider's rights.

Batching economics must follow the applicable rule rather than a spreadsheet's desire to spread fees across many claims. Validate parties, service characteristics, service dates, and the currently operative batching requirements before combining disputes; requirements and implementation can change through rulemaking and litigation. Track the 90-calendar-day suspension affecting subsequent initiation by the same initiating party for the same or similar items or services involving the same opposing party. Evaluate the associated post-suspension initiation provision instead of assuming every held claim becomes permanently unavailable. A cooling-off register should retain the determination date, affected counterparties, service grouping rationale, and next permitted action. Do not treat a code match alone as a complete legal test. For each proposed batch, reserve the nonrefundable administrative charge and the certified-entity fee using the applicable published schedule. The prevailing party generally receives its certified-entity fee back, while the nonprevailing party bears that fee; settlement and administrative dispositions require separate reconciliation. Budget dismissed or ineligible matters with no assumed refund until the actual disposition and applicable refund rules establish one. This conservative cash treatment prevents a pending refund receivable from disguising a loss-making book or financing the next filing prematurely.

Maintain separate fields for initial allowed payment, disclosed QPA, patient responsibility, selected offer, additional payer obligation, cleared additional cash, returned funds, administrative charges, entity charges, refunds, and casework expense. The QPA is not automatically the initial payment, and neither number automatically equals the final out-of-network rate. Use the actual initial-payment baseline when calculating incremental recovery. Define eligible contingency base as cleared incremental cash minus unrecovered dispute fees and agreed external casework costs, floored at zero. Subtract a refund from unrecovered costs only when received or otherwise contractually settled with adequate evidence. If a $20,000 selected total payment amount implies $10,000 above the established baseline but only $6,000 arrives, a $1,200 unrecovered cost balance leaves $4,800 currently eligible for sharing. At 25%, invoice $1,200 rather than $2,500. Allocate lawful patient cost sharing and prior payments before calculating that additional obligation; the example assumes both already reconciled. Provider-funded expense reimbursements are tracked separately from the operator's earned share and are not quietly added to canonical revenue. Internal labor and operating overhead then reduce operator profit without deducting the same external case cost twice. Reversals require a contractual true-up, with credit notes tied to the original claim and invoice.

sections.heading: 3. Choose a settlement rail that proves receipt without creating a second collection problem
paragraphs: Default to payer payment into the provider's established account, followed by a separately authorized operator invoice. This preserves the ordinary claims-payment chain and avoids turning the recovery firm into an unnecessary custodian of medical receivables. For healthcare EFT and ERA, use the adopted transaction standards and reassociation data, including the ACH CCD+ payment information and matching 835 trace information where applicable. A bank credit without allocation evidence is unresolved cash, while an 835 without a corresponding settled deposit is not collection. Reconcile both before computing the contingency share. If the payer uses a virtual card, assess processing deductions and available payment alternatives rather than letting convenience shrink the provider's net recovery invisibly. For any banking change, use a callback to a previously validated contact, dual approval, and a retained change log. Do not place clinical narratives or patient names in ACH descriptions, wire references, card receipts, or payment-platform memos. Use a restricted internal case token and maintain the protected mapping inside the authorized claim system. The BAA and secure EDI pipeline cover permitted handling of protected information; they do not authorize publishing patient details to a payment vendor that lacks the required contractual and security arrangements.

Payment rails solve different problems, and eight alternatives deserve explicit comparison. A wire accelerates a known settlement but does not cure an insolvent counterparty. ACH supports routine payer and provider transfers, but authorization, returns, bank reconciliation, and remittance linkage still matter. Escrow can reduce performance risk when both parties actually agree to a funded arrangement administered by a suitable independent custodian; federal IDR does not automatically create escrow. A retainer or expense reserve finances case preparation, not a recovery already earned. Statutory disbursement describes the payment obligation following the determination, not a distinct government-operated bank rail or public guarantee. Platform checkout is usually better suited to the provider's service invoice than to moving underlying medical benefits. Factoring exchanges a receivable for discounted liquidity and may introduce recourse, assignment restrictions, servicing duties, and UCC priority questions. Milestone holds can allocate vendor-performance risk, but a private arrangement cannot unilaterally extend the payer's statutory payment deadline. Select the smallest workable arrangement, documenting payer acceptance and the provider's treasury instructions. If the operator cannot explain who owns the funds at every stage, abandon that routing design and restore direct provider collection with a transparent service-fee invoice.

Fee protection belongs in the engagement contract and evidence trail rather than in surprise liens or unrestricted account access. Define covered inventory, exclusions, the baseline methodology, expense allocation, collection verification, invoicing dates, payment authorization, termination, and dispute resolution. A narrowly drafted collection tail may preserve fees on specifically identified work completed before termination; it should not claim every future payer dollar. Require periodic remittance exports, access to relevant settlement correspondence, and an obligation to report direct payments and offsets. Prohibit duplicate contingency charges where another recovery vendor already owns the assignment. Review applicable state restrictions on collection activity, professional fee sharing, and receivable assignments before choosing the compensation and custody structure. If the provider refuses automatic debit, use ordinary accounts payable with a clear payment period and limited audit rights. A $1,800 earned invoice paid thirty days late creates a working-capital burden, not a reason to collect from the patient or divert payer money. Suspend new elective work for persistent vendor nonpayment while preserving agreed duties on active deadlines and arranging an orderly handoff. When escrow is justified, release conditions should name the exact evidence required and an independent dispute mechanism instead of letting either party freeze all funds indefinitely.

sections.heading: 4. Underwrite counterparties, acquisition costs, and the three canonical profit cases
paragraphs: Credit screening has two targets: the party funding benefits and the provider purchasing recovery services. Review issuer licensing and public regulatory orders through the relevant state insurance department, supplemented by available statutory statements and observed payment behavior. For self-funded plans, inspect accessible plan disclosures and Form 5500 information where applicable, while recognizing that historical filings do not prove today's funding availability. Ask the administrator how settlement instructions reach the funding account and where exceptions are resolved. For the provider, review aging, ownership changes, insolvency indicators, existing vendor disputes, and prior payment references obtained with authorization. A strong payer does not prevent a distressed practice from withholding the operator's invoice. Set exposure limits by payer family, provider group, fee reserve, and unresolved award age. Track dollars outstanding rather than only claim counts, since one concentrated specialty portfolio can dominate working capital. If $50,000 of incremental obligations are outstanding and only $35,000 has cleared, collect and report the $35,000; the remaining $15,000 stays a receivable, not cash-backed contingency revenue. Reduce new filing exposure when aging worsens, but keep existing procedural commitments staffed. A practical stop-loss protects filing capital without abandoning a provider at a live deadline.

The second specified play, llm_citation_geo_poisoning, is implemented only as factual Generative Engine Optimization and AI-Overview Citation Seeding. Its identifier is not permission to manipulate private retrieval systems, fabricate endorsements, or plant instructions that override another assistant's behavior. Observe public citations across commercial buyer prompts in ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews, recording query, date, cited page, and factual coverage gaps. Publish visible comparison tables on owned pages and pursue legitimate editorial placements in relevant trade publications; use schema.org JSON-LD only when it accurately describes visible content. No placement guarantees inclusion or a default recommendation. For an illustrative acquisition cohort, spend $1,200 producing and distributing a substantiated eligibility guide, generate twelve qualified inquiries, and sign three providers: acquisition cost is $400 per signed provider. If their first measured cohort produces $9,000 of earned contingency revenue before internal operating costs, the revenue-to-acquisition-spend ratio is 7.5, not a profit margin. Measure actual attribution and collection lag before expanding. Fallback means corroborated, independent publications and useful factual datasets, not hidden text or invented outcomes. Publish aggregate operating examples without patient identifiers, and label illustrative economics so prospective buyers cannot mistake modeled recovery for documented client cash.

Reconcile the business to Formula v2.0 without substituting awards, provider receipts, or financed receivables for earned contingency revenue. Conservative revenue of $110,000 less $77,000 of operating costs produces $33,000 owner net profit at 30%; staffing is 1 FT + 2 C. Base revenue of $505,000 less $287,850 produces $217,150 at 43.0%, with the same staffing configuration. Scaled revenue of $900,000 less $396,000 produces $504,000 at 56%, with 2 FT + 3 C. These annual costs include the complete modeled operating burden; the stated $1,800–$10,500 monthly operating range is not a substitute for annual scenario reconciliation. At a uniform illustrative 25% share, those revenues require $440,000, $2,020,000, and $3,600,000 of collected incremental fee bases after the specified external deductions. Actual mixes of 20–35% contracts change required recovery volume, not the canonical profit targets. Keep startup capital of $10,000–$45,000 separate from recurring profit, and plan around the stated one-to-four-month first-deal window rather than immediate cash. Gross provider collections remain outside the operator's revenue ledger; assess principal-versus-agent presentation for any separately billed pass-throughs. Scale only when cash conversion, provider payment discipline, and deadline capacity support the modeled contribution with the stated small team.

chapters.question_prompt: What are the real unit economics, gross-to-net margin deductions, scrub/reversal reserves, and working-capital float requirements for no surprises act (idr) medical arbitration & out-of-network recovery?
chapters.title: Unit Economics, Margin Waterfall & Working-Capital Float
chapters.subtitle: 835 ERA Reconciliation, Cash-Earned Contingencies, Federal IDR Fee Exposure, and Provider-Funded Float
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #45, No Surprises Act (IDR) Medical Arbitration & Out-of-Network Recovery, ranks #09 of 49 with a 94/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Across the series' 12 mapped plays, this chapter isolates cash-earned recovery economics and the adjacent DME acquisition model. The canonical annual owner profits are $33,000 Conservative, $217,150 Base, and $504,000 Scaled, against operator revenue of $110,000, $505,000, and $900,000. Those revenues exclude initial provider payments, unpaid awards, and supplier reimbursement. A worked cohort deducts administrative fees, unrecovered entity fees, and direct casework before applying the contingency share. Separate operating waterfalls expose delivery labor, acquisition spending, reversal provisions, and financing. The decisive constraint is liquidity: provider-funded filing expenses and disciplined cash matching prevent a profitable award pipeline from exhausting payroll.

sections.heading: 1. Convert provider collections into a cash-earned contingency base
paragraphs: Start with the 835 electronic remittance advice, the payer's initial payment, and the matching bank deposit, not the provider's charge master. The qualifying payment amount, or QPA, is a statutory benchmark; it is not necessarily the initial allowed amount or actual remittance. Preserve those fields separately. For each claim, calculate incremental payer cash as subsequently collected reimbursement above the documented initial payer payment, excluding patient money and unrelated adjustments. Then subtract nonrefundable CMS administrative fees, unrecovered certified entity fees, and attributable casework before applying the contracted share. The illustrative share here is 25%, not a prescribed market rate. A negative case balance remains attached to its contractually defined cohort; do not erase losses by moving winning claims into a fresh invoice. Provider collections remain provider revenue, while the operator records only its earned service fee. Under an ASC 606 principal-versus-agent assessment, custody of provider funds alone does not make the operator principal for medical services. Treat the retained economic share as 25% of the eligible net recovery pool, never 25% of provider gross billings. This boundary makes the scorecard's revenue figures interpretable and prevents a second, fictitious medical-revenue business from appearing in the management accounts.

Consider 100 intake claims with $100,000 of initial provider payments already collected and excluded. Eligibility review identifies 60 potentially federal claims; negotiation and economic screening leave 40 filings. Assume 28 favorable determinations, eight losses, and four eligibility dismissals. Each favorable determination represents $2,500 of incremental reimbursement, producing $70,000 of awarded uplift, but only 24 have paid: incremental cash is $60,000. For arithmetic only, budget $100 administrative expense and $500 entity expense per filing; these are planning assumptions, not current fee quotations. Initial disbursements are $4,000 administrative, $20,000 entity, and $6,000 direct casework, or $30,000. Assume documented entity refunds of $14,000 for the 28 prevailing cases, leaving $6,000 unrecovered. Budget dismissal deposits as fully exposed until the applicable entity policy and actual refund establish otherwise; dismissal treatment must be checked rather than inferred from winning-party treatment. Net cash eligible for sharing is $60,000 minus $4,000 minus $6,000 minus $6,000, equaling $44,000. The operator earns $11,000; the provider retains $33,000 after those costs and that fee. The four unpaid favorable determinations contribute no contingency revenue yet. A later receipt or refund requires a cumulative cohort true-up, not a duplicate fee calculation.

The annual bridge below preserves the canonical scorecard without pretending that every portfolio repeats the sample cohort's payer mix. Conservative collects $600,000 of uplift and deducts $160,000 before sharing; Base collects $2,700,000 and deducts $680,000; Scaled collects $4,800,000 and deducts $1,200,000. At 25%, eligible pools of $440,000, $2,020,000, and $3,600,000 produce exactly $110,000, $505,000, and $900,000 of operator revenue. These upstream costs are provider-borne amounts under the illustrative agreement, funded from a restricted expense balance or deducted from recoveries. They are not operator revenue and are not deducted again in the operating waterfall. Direct casework here means separately reimbursed, claim-specific external work; operator delivery labor means unreimbursed internal management, collection follow-up, quality control, and contractor capacity. Give each invoice line exactly one classification. Require a contractual loss-carryforward rule, refund ownership rule, and settlement statement before launching a cohort. Otherwise a winning determination can trigger a fee despite an aggregate provider loss. Use claim identifiers, payer references, and bank transaction identifiers to reconcile cumulative earned fees against amounts already invoiced, with a documented exception queue for reversals and unmatched deposits.

callout.body: The highest-value reconciliation work happens between the 835 adjustment, the bank deposit, and the cumulative provider settlement statement.

sections.heading: 2. Reconcile earned fees to owner profit without hiding labor or reversals
paragraphs: Once the cash-earned fee enters the operator ledger, the second waterfall measures the cost of running the recovery company. Conservative deducts $77,000 from $110,000, leaving $33,000 and a 30% margin. Base deducts $287,850 from $505,000, leaving $217,150 and a 43.0% margin. Scaled deducts $396,000 from $900,000, leaving $504,000 and a 56% margin. These are the canonical annual outcomes; the category allocations below are illustrative budgets that reconcile exactly, not claimed historical expense observations. Owner profit means operating earnings available to the working owner before personal income taxes, debt principal repayments, and distributions. It includes compensation for that owner's own full-time effort; subtract a replacement salary separately when comparing this business with passive investments. Conservative and Base each use one full-time owner plus two contractors. Scaled uses that owner, one additional employee, and three contractors. Its delivery budget includes the additional employee's loaded compensation and contractor payments. Contractor count does not imply full-time availability. The operating plan must translate the dollar budget into contracted hours, expected claim touches, and overflow arrangements before assuming the margin improvement is achievable.

Delivery spending of $32,000, $125,000, and $190,000 must buy specific capacity rather than an abstract automation percentage. An illustrative $50 hourly loaded rate purchases 640, 2,500, and 3,800 paid-equivalent hours annually; the Scaled conversion is a blended capacity measure because its payroll includes an employee. At 1.5 hours per completed workflow, those budgets support approximately 427, 1,667, and 2,533 workflow equivalents, excluding the separately reimbursed external casework already deducted upstream. Measure actual touches for eligibility classification, brief assembly, remittance matching, and unpaid-award escalation. An 835 CARC/RARC parser can triage underpayments, but ERISA status and federal eligibility require plan and service evidence; remittance codes alone cannot establish jurisdiction. Acquisition budgets of $15,000, $60,000, and $85,000 could represent 10, 30, and 50 activated provider accounts, implying acquisition costs of $1,500, $2,000, and $1,700. Those account counts are planning assumptions, not canonical scorecard inputs. Allocate outbound labor, conference spending, and referral-channel administration consistently. Calculate payback using collected contribution after delivery costs rather than the face value of a newly signed provider's backlog. If an account supplies ineligible claims, stop paid acquisition until its service mix is corrected.

The scrub and reversal provisions are $6,000, $25,250, and $18,000, equivalent to approximately 5.45%, 5%, and 2% of earned operator revenue. They are economic loss allowances within these planning margins, not a second cash fee deducted from the provider's sharing pool. Cover identifiable fee refunds, post-payment recoupments, duplicate recovery corrections, and unreimbursed remediation after preventable eligibility errors. Rejected intake that never generates a fee reduces conversion; it does not create revenue followed by an invented reversal. Likewise, an unpaid award has no earned fee to reserve against in this model. Maintain a separate exposure register for fee receivables earned on provider cash but awaiting operator remittance. The accountant should determine whether each realized event belongs in contra-revenue, credit loss, or expense; the management waterfall must count it once regardless of presentation. Ring-fencing equivalent cash is a liquidity policy, not another profit deduction. Scaled's 2% assumption requires evidence from mature cohorts, not confidence in a brief generator. If its observed loss rate remains 5%, the extra $27,000 reduces owner profit to $477,000. Record that deterioration immediately rather than preserving the headline margin by releasing reserves before payer recoupment exposure has matured.

sections.heading: 3. Fund the collection clock before expanding the filing queue
paragraphs: Run two clocks: the statutory dispute clock and the economic collection clock. Federal open negotiation generally lasts 30 business days, and initiation generally follows within four business days after that period ends, subject to applicable extensions and current process instructions. Neither interval guarantees cash. Model eligibility review, negotiation, entity selection, submissions, determination, payer payment, bank matching, and provider-to-operator remittance separately. The federal framework requires payment of the determined amount within 30 calendar days after determination, but actual delinquency still needs collection capacity and cash reserves. Use a 90-day Conservative, 120-day Base, and 90-day Scaled cash-conversion planning lag from funded work to usable operator receipts. These are stress-model assumptions, not reported industry averages or legal extensions. Because fees are earned only on recovered cash here, most pre-collection pipeline value is unearned contingent opportunity rather than accounts receivable. Report that aging separately from genuine invoice DSO after provider collection. A provider payment lock of 15 days would extend a 105-day operating cycle to the Base model's 120 days. Do not add that lock again when sizing liquidity. Weekly aging should identify who currently controls the next action and the exact evidence needed to release payment.

For a launch-period funding test, remove the noncash economic provision from operating deductions while retaining budgeted financing cash expense. Annual cash operating spend becomes $71,000 Conservative, $262,600 Base, and $378,000 Scaled. Dividing by twelve gives monthly burn of $5,916.67, $21,883.33, and $31,500. Using 30-day planning months, the assumed lags require $17,750, $87,533.33, and $94,500 of operating bridge cash. Add a separately ring-fenced reversal cushion of $6,000, $25,250, and $18,000 to obtain liquidity targets of $23,750, $112,783.33, and $112,500, excluding provider-funded claim expenses, startup purchases, taxes, and owner distributions. This conservative launch test assumes no usable receipts during the stated funding interval; a mature staggered portfolio should instead use a weekly receipts-and-payments forecast. An extra 30 days adds $5,916.67, $21,883.33, or $31,500 before additional interest. The stated $10,000–$45,000 startup capital range can support a staged Conservative launch, not automatic Base throughput. Likewise, the $1,800–$10,500 monthly overhead envelope is not the fully loaded scaled burn once acquisition and delivery capacity are included. Bridge the difference with retained earnings, smaller cohorts, or committed financing rather than supplier invoices left unpaid.

Keep filing float outside the operator's unrestricted payroll account. The worked 100-intake cohort needs $30,000 of initial provider-funded disbursements even though its eventual net upstream expense is $16,000 after entity refunds. Requiring only $16,000 at inception leaves a $14,000 timing hole. Document replenishment thresholds, refund ownership, and permission to debit specific expenses; reconcile provider balances individually rather than lending one practice's funds to another. If the operator advances expenses, record the resulting contractual reimbursement asset separately, test collectibility, and add the peak advance to the liquidity forecast. For illustration, financing a $30,000 advance for 120 days at 18% simple annual interest costs approximately $1,775 using a 365-day year, before facility charges. That increment must fit the financing budget or reduce profit. QuickBooks or Xero can hold provider control accounts, while a PostgreSQL ledger links claims, filings, refunds, and deposits; execute required business associate agreements before vendors handle protected health information. Maintain a 13-week cash forecast with actual receipt dates and a separate forward pipeline schedule. When cash headroom falls below the next payroll plus committed filing obligations, reduce new intake immediately while protecting existing statutory deadlines and collection follow-up.

sections.heading: 4. Stress collections, reject weak filings, and separate DME acquisition economics
paragraphs: Stress cash conversion before debating the upside of higher offers. Holding upstream expenses and operator budgets fixed, a 10% decline in incremental payer cash reduces eligible pools by $60,000, $270,000, and $480,000. At 25%, fee revenue falls $15,000, $67,500, and $120,000, leaving owner profits of $18,000, $149,650, and $384,000. A 20% delivery-cost overrun alone removes $6,400, $25,000, and $38,000, leaving $26,600, $192,150, and $466,000. Combining both shocks produces $11,600, $124,650, and $346,000. These tests hold the dollar provisions fixed to expose isolated shocks; re-estimate them if losses also change. For individual filing decisions, use a probability-weighted cash test rather than published prevailing-offer percentages. An illustrative case with a $2,500 collectible uplift, 70% favorable probability, and 85% conditional collection probability has $1,487.50 expected incremental cash. Subtract a $100 administrative assumption, $150 expected entity loss on a $500 deposit with 30% loss probability, and $150 casework: expected shareable value is $1,087.50 and the 25% operator participation is $271.88. Additional eligibility-dismissal risk, collection expense, or prolonged float can consume that contribution. Reject negative expected contribution before incurring a filing fee, while preserving records explaining the decision.

The mapped play out_of_network_dme_telehealth_billing_arbitrage, TRACK_1, combines an MSO, patient acquisition, independent telehealth clinicians, and licensed DME or reference-laboratory suppliers. Its stated acquisition range is $85–$220 per patient, reimbursement range $900–$3,500+, and hardware cost range $70–$220. Those figures describe adjacent supplier economics, not federal IDR eligibility or operator contingency revenue. At $1,500 collected supplier reimbursement, $150 hardware cost, $150 acquisition cost, $200 fulfillment and clinical-support cost, and $150 denial or recoupment provision, illustrative supplier contribution is $850 before remaining overhead and MSO charges. Increasing acquisition cost to $220 reduces it to $780. At the downside combination of $900 reimbursement, $220 hardware, $220 acquisition, $200 support, and a $90 provision, only $170 remains. A separate $6,000 monthly fair-market-value MSO retainer spread across 100 supported patients represents $60 of operator revenue per patient for management analysis; it is not a per-referral contractual fee. Favor recurring CGM resupply and commercial payer contracts only where coverage, authorization, and clinical necessity support them. If clinical review rejects a proposed device or test, stop that acquisition path rather than seeking a different prescriber to validate the sale.

Keep that adjacent play in a separate ledger and legal structure assessment. Most standalone DME or telehealth transactions do not become federal No Surprises Act disputes merely because they are out of network. Screen service category, location, plan funding, applicable state law, and any valid statutory exception before filing. Self-funded ERISA status is relevant but not a complete eligibility determination. For MSO arrangements, evaluate 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b), the personal-services safe harbor at 42 CFR § 1001.952(d), and physician self-referral requirements under 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn where applicable. A flat fair-market-value retainer alone does not satisfy every safe-harbor element; services must be genuine, commercially reasonable, and structured without prohibited referral incentives. Commercial business also requires state fee-splitting, licensing, and payer-contract review. Require independent third-party chart review and preserve clinician control over necessity. For the IDR core, verify current batching criteria and the 90-calendar-day same-party, same-or-similar-service cooling restriction, including applicable exceptions and subsequent filing windows. Do not aggregate dissimilar codes merely to dilute entity expense. FAIR Health benchmarks and clinical acuity evidence can support a properly documented submission, but automated briefs cannot replace eligibility evidence or make barred billed-charge material permissible. When federal jurisdiction fails, route to the applicable state process or ordinary contractual collection workflow.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #45, No Surprises Act (IDR) Medical Arbitration & Out-of-Network Recovery, ranks #09 of 49 with a 94/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Across its 12 mapped plays, the investable advantage is disciplined recovery infrastructure, not an expensive claims platform. Allocate $10,000–$45,000 with at least half preserved for working capital, then configure a twelve-layer stack around eligibility, business-day clocks, evidence, and cash reconciliation. The canonical annual owner profits are $33,000 Conservative, $217,150 Base, and $504,000 Scaled. Those outcomes use earned contingency revenue, never provider collections or pharmacy reimbursement. This chapter separates refundable deposits from expenses, prices a lean operating envelope, and isolates the mapped 340B pharmacy play behind its own inventory, eligibility, and service-contract economics.

sections.heading: 1. Protect liquidity before buying capacity
paragraphs: Start with a segregated launch ledger, not an annual software shopping list. The $10,000 configuration below reserves $5,500, or 55%, while the $45,000 configuration reserves $25,000, or 55.6%. Both exceed the 50% working-capital requirement before any filing begins. These reserves cover collection delays, temporary entity-fee deposits, and operating interruptions; they are not permission to subsidize every provider dispute. Require the provider agreement to allocate CMS administrative fees, certified-entity deposits, unrecovered charges, and casework reimbursements explicitly. Prefer provider-funded dispute costs with a separate reconciliation ledger rather than unlimited operator advances. At $1,800 monthly recurring expense, $5,500 buys approximately 3.1 months before deposits; at $10,500, $25,000 buys only 2.4 months. Since the first deal can take one to four months and an award can take longer to become cash, the upper spending envelope requires contracted volume or additional liquidity. Release each nonreserve allocation against a deliverable: executed agreements, a restore-tested workspace, a validated remittance parser, or a qualified provider pipeline. Do not exhaust the integration allocation on custom payer connectors before a representative 835 file has demonstrated recoverable claims. Record vendor cancellation dates beside committed cash so annual subscriptions cannot silently consume the next filing cycle.

Treat the $1,800–$10,500 monthly range as recurring operating infrastructure and retained support, not the entire annual expense base. A lean $1,800 planning month allocates $120 to licenses, $180 to infrastructure, $200 to insurance, $150 to bookkeeping and administration, $850 to contractor availability, and $300 to security and quality checks. A $10,500 operating month can allocate $1,000 to tools and infrastructure, $500 to insurance and administration, $3,000 to coordination, $2,000 to coding expertise, $2,000 to specialist counsel, and $2,000 to security and quality operations. These are spending envelopes, not vendor quotations or guaranteed staffing rates. Variable production labor and other portfolio expenses must still fit the canonical annual cost ceilings. Conservative revenue of $110,000 permits $77,000 of total expenses; Base revenue of $505,000 permits $287,850; Scaled revenue of $900,000 permits $396,000. Do not add recurring expense a second time after calculating those totals. Use a thirteen-week cash forecast with separate columns for recognized fees, bank receipts, refundable deposits, provider-funded costs, and payroll commitments. If collections slip two weeks, pause discretionary acquisition and software expansion first. Preserve eligibility screening and deadline coverage, because missed filings destroy assets rather than merely delaying administrative work.

Establish the contracting entity, obtain an EIN through the IRS, and maintain separate operating, tax, and reserve accounts using an FDIC-insured bank whose actual account ownership and insurance coverage have been checked. A fintech interface is not itself evidence of deposit insurance. Document bank signers, payment limits, vendor onboarding, and dual authorization for changes to provider remittance instructions. Keep provider recoveries flowing directly to the provider whenever possible; invoice the earned contingency after bank-level reconciliation instead of pooling patient or provider money in the operating account. Engage a bookkeeper who can distinguish a refundable deposit asset from an expense and a reimbursed disbursement from earned revenue. Bind professional liability and cyber coverage suited to healthcare claims services, checking exclusions for billing disputes, subcontractors, social engineering, and contractual obligations. Obtain specialist review of representative authority, state collection-agency requirements, and any legal work that requires licensed counsel. Execute the provider services agreement and HIPAA business associate agreement before receiving protected health information. Contractors receive written confidentiality, access, incident-reporting, and deletion obligations, with subcontractor BAAs where required. None of this requires premium offices or enterprise procurement staff; it requires signed documents, accountable owners, and evidence that money and sensitive records cannot move through informal channels.

callout.title: Buy liquidity and error prevention before dashboard polish
callout.body: The earliest durable advantage is a clean cost waterfall, a recoverable evidence trail, and enough cash to survive payer delays.
items: Require provider-funded deposits before submission; cap operator advances by provider and payer rather than by salesperson confidence.
Keep the certified-entity deposit receivable open until the refund reaches the bank; a favorable determination does not replenish cash immediately.
Request three representative 835 remittances and their EOB counterparts before quoting a recovery engagement; preserve CAS adjustments, CARC, and RARC context.
Purchase FAIR Health benchmark access only after confirming permitted evidentiary use and case relevance; clinical-acuity documentation often exposes the real evidence gap first.

sections.heading: 2. Build twelve layers without twelve enterprise contracts
paragraphs: Use the twelve-layer matrix as a procurement architecture, not an instruction to activate every service immediately. Its exact dollar figures are explicit planning assumptions based on named tiers and standard list-price structures, not verified current quotations. Confirm current terms, region, annual commitments, eligible services, and BAA coverage before purchase; taxes, support, egress, implementation, and hosting can change the invoice. With two Microsoft 365 Business Premium seats at $22 each, two Bitwarden Teams seats at $4 each, two GitHub Team seats at $4 each, and two Tailscale Starter users at $6 each, the modeled fixed subtotal is $72 monthly. Add 100 GB of S3 Standard storage at $0.023 per GB-month and 10,000 Textract text-detection pages at $0.0015 each: the narrow subtotal becomes $89.30 before requests and other costs. This is a component calculation, not a complete HIPAA-ready operating budget. The $120 license and $180 infrastructure envelopes leave room for operational requirements that list prices omit. Start with structured ERA ingestion rather than OCR whenever possible. Text extraction cannot establish jurisdiction, interpret every adjustment code, or prove that an award was paid. Free software also consumes maintenance time, so retire overlapping tools when a covered existing service already performs the same task.

Separate the workspace into protected case records, internal operational controls, and public commercial material. Microsoft 365 and AWS receive protected records only after the relevant agreements, service eligibility, configuration, and minimum-necessary access have been established. A vendor's healthcare marketing page does not establish that every product feature falls within its BAA. GitHub contains source code and synthetic fixtures, never production remittances. Sentry receives opaque job identifiers and sanitized errors, never patient names, diagnosis descriptions, payer member identifiers, document excerpts, or signed download links. Cloudflare serves the public website only in this design; its free tier does not become a patient-document proxy. Password vault entries identify systems rather than patients. Use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where supported, separate administrator identities, device encryption, conditional access, and role-specific case permissions. A coordinator should not change payment instructions, and a developer should not need production charts to repair parsing logic. Export audit records to a restricted location and define retention from the records' purpose, contractual duties, and applicable requirements. Maintain required HIPAA policy documentation for its applicable retention period without assuming every clinical artifact has the same rule. Test account termination with a contractor identity before actual offboarding becomes urgent.

Build the case ledger around immutable source references and reproducible calculations. Store the original 835, EOB, negotiation notice, proof of transmission, offers, determination, deposit receipts, and subsequent bank evidence under one internal case identifier. Preserve payer and plan identifiers separately: a familiar insurer logo does not establish whether the benefit arrangement is insured or self-funded. Python can normalize ERA segments and PostgreSQL can enforce unique claim keys, but neither replaces a documented exception queue. Send ambiguous CAS adjustments, missing dates, duplicate payments, and contradictory plan evidence to a named reviewer. Generate briefs from versioned templates and clinician-approved facts; do not let a language model invent acuity, network participation, or contracting history. Use LibreOffice locally for controlled document assembly if the endpoint is managed, avoiding an additional online PDF processor. Self-hosted DocuSeal belongs on patched infrastructure for business contracting; the free software license does not include hosting, security operations, or protected-record handling. Define recovery-point and recovery-time objectives in hours, then perform a restore into an isolated environment. A second encrypted backup under a separate administrative boundary protects against both deletion and account compromise. Monthly maintenance must include dependency updates, access review, restore evidence, and a sample reconciliation from raw remittance through final invoice.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile recovery economics and isolate the 340B adjacency
paragraphs: Anchor every revenue forecast to incremental cash actually received above the payer's initial QPA or allowed remittance, not the provider's billed charges or the amount offered in arbitration. For this chapter's illustrative contract, define eligible recovery as the positive incremental cash balance after nonrefundable administrative fees, unrecovered certified-entity fees, and contractually allocated casework costs. Apply the contingency percentage to that balance, with a floor of zero. The canonical scorecard does not prescribe a contingency percentage; using 20% solely for capacity planning requires $550,000, $2,525,000, and $4,500,000 of annual eligible recovery to produce Conservative, Base, and Scaled operator revenue respectively. Actual incremental provider receipts must exceed those amounts by the deducted costs. Keep baseline collections outside operator revenue, and do not label a provider's gross recovery as an ASC 606 fee. Evaluate principal-versus-agent treatment for reimbursed disbursements separately; cash passing through a bank account does not establish a performance obligation or earned revenue. The canonical margins then reconcile exactly: $110,000 less $77,000 equals $33,000; $505,000 less $287,850 equals $217,150; $900,000 less $396,000 equals $504,000. Those expense totals include operating costs once. Provider-paid deductions used to define the fee base are not automatically a second operator expense.

Stress-test one collected case before extrapolating a portfolio. Suppose the initial allowed payment was $2,000 and total cash eventually reaches $5,000. Incremental cash is $3,000. For this example only, assume a $115 administrative charge, a $600 entity deposit, and $385 of provider-paid casework; these are budgeting inputs, not assertions of current federal or entity prices. If the provider prevails and the full entity deposit is returned, eligible recovery equals $3,000 minus $115 minus $385, or $2,500. A 20% contingency earns $500, leaving $2,000 of incremental benefit after those costs and the operator fee. Until the deposit refund is received, the ledger shows $600 of tied-up cash and excludes it from available liquidity. A loss with no additional payment yields no contingency and can consume $1,100 if the administrative charge, entity fee, and casework are unrecovered. Budget ineligibility dismissals for full fee loss unless the applicable disposition rules establish a refund; never assume dismissal makes the deposit recoverable. Maintain separate counts for initiated cases, eligible cases, determinations, awards, collections, and reconciled refunds. An 80% favorable-determination rate cannot substitute for the proportion of submitted cases that produce collected, cost-adjusted cash within the modeled period.

The mapped play section_340b_contract_pharmacy_spread_arbitrage belongs in this capital chapter because pharmacy inventory can silently consume the entire IDR reserve. Across the volume's 12 mapped plays, this adjacency requires separate underwriting rather than a blended revenue claim. Partner only with an eligible, registered covered entity, such as a qualifying FQHC, Ryan White grantee, or qualifying hospital; rural location alone establishes nothing. A hypothetical specialty prescription with $10,000 acquisition reference cost, $6,000 eligible 340B acquisition cost, and $9,000 actual reimbursement produces $3,000 before dispensing, administration, reversals, and other charges. The 40% modeled acquisition reduction is not a universal statutory discount, and reimbursement is never automatically 100% of a reference price. A support operator charging a documented $150 flat administrative fee earns $150, not the $3,000 spread or the $9,000 reimbursement. Separate TPA split-billing, specialty fulfillment, and tele-referral arrangements, testing patient eligibility, diversion prevention, Medicaid duplicate discounts, and federal remuneration restrictions. If manufacturer restrictions block contract-pharmacy access, assess a genuinely entity-owned pharmacy and required 340B ESP submissions where applicable; neither guarantees access to restricted NDCs. Apply strict EHR encounter checks before replenishment. When eligibility or access remains unresolved, stop replenishment and preserve IDR liquidity rather than financing speculative drug inventory.

sections.heading: 4. Prove eligibility, clocks, evidence, and cash before launch
paragraphs: Pre-flight begins with jurisdiction, because paying a filing fee does not make a dispute eligible. Identify the service, coverage type, plan funding, relevant state law, provider status, and whether federal surprise-billing protections govern the item. ERISA status alone is not a complete routing rule: distinguish self-funded plans from insured coverage, evaluate specified state-law applicability and permitted elections, and recognize excluded programs and services. Obtain plan evidence rather than inferring funding from the payer's logo or an ERA adjustment. Under the federal framework, the open-negotiation initiation window generally runs for 30 business days from receipt of the initial payment or denial; the negotiation period itself is a separate 30-business-day interval. The federal IDR initiation window generally follows for four business days. That four-day window is not a universal deadline for selecting a certified entity or assembling every batch. Encode each event with its own legal trigger, service evidence, calendar definition, and applicable extension. Maintain a holiday-aware business-day calculator and require an independent human deadline check. Track the 90-calendar-day suspension for the initiating party's same-party, same-or-similar disputes and the applicable subsequent filing window. Batch only under rules operative for the filing date, preserving the authority used for every eligibility decision.

Construct the evidence packet before escalating a claim from negotiation to paid submission. The packet needs the initial remittance, QPA information supplied by the plan, a defensible offer, clinical facts, negotiation history, jurisdiction support, and proof of timely action. FAIR Health data can inform an analyst, but the federal statute excludes certain considerations, including usual and customary charges, billed charges, and public-payer rates, from the certified entity's determination. Do not repackage excluded charge information as a permissible acuity argument. Link each offered fact to an allowed consideration and actual records, and have qualified staff resolve coding or clinical disputes. Use the applicable current guidance rather than assuming that a historical template survived litigation or rule changes unchanged. After a determination, establish the payment obligation and track the generally applicable 30-calendar-day payment period from the determination date. An unpaid award remains a collection task, not earned cash-based contingency revenue. Reconcile payer remittances, bank deposits, offsets, recoupments, and deposit refunds independently. Keep escalation correspondence and supporting records ready for the appropriate enforcement channel when payment is overdue. Recalculate the fee if a reversal changes incremental collected cash. The operator invoice should let the provider reproduce the baseline, uplift, deductions, percentage, and final charge without opening a sales presentation.

Run a supervised rehearsal using synthetic records, then a small authorized pilot with real provider files. Include an insured state-law claim, an ambiguous self-funded plan, a late negotiation trigger, an invalid proposed batch, a duplicate ERA, a losing determination, an unpaid favorable determination, and a refunded deposit. The software must route uncertainty to review rather than manufacturing eligibility. Verify that reminders reach a primary owner and backup, that access revocation blocks an old session, and that restored records retain their links to the case ledger. Reconcile the pilot against the provider's bank evidence before issuing its first contingency invoice. Measure rejection rate, minutes per eligible case, administrative cost per initiation, entity-fee losses, days from determination to receipt, and actual fee realization by payer. Use those observations to decide whether a second contractor should handle intake or clinical evidence; adding staff to the wrong bottleneck merely increases fixed burn. Keep the initial provider cohort narrow enough that one person can inspect every exception while another covers deadlines. Authorize growth only when the thirteen-week forecast remains positive after a delayed-payment stress case and all four verification checks below pass. If a check fails, repair the specific defect and continue safe preparatory work without sending unsupported disputes or exposing additional records.
